pages.why: The flat half adds no area but doubles the length. So the average halves, to about 104 V. That is 0.318 of the 325 V peak, the peak ÷ π.

pages.name: Which way now?
pages.task: Which way does current flow through the load now?
pages.answer: Down, the same way as in the positive half
pages.why: In the negative half, the supply's other wire is the high one. D3 takes the current to the top of the load. D4 returns it from the bottom. So it flows down, as before. Each pair conducts while the other blocks.

pages.task: A bridge feeds a 12 V battery charger. How much lower is its output than with perfect diodes?
pages.why: At every moment the current passes through two diodes in series. Each holds about 0.7 V. So the bridge takes about 1.4 V. On a 207 V output that is under 1%. On 12 V it is about 12%.

pages.name: A 115 V bridge
pages.task: A bridge runs from a 115 V single-phase supply. What reverse voltage must each diode withstand?
pages.why: While a diode blocks, the conducting pair joins it straight across the supply. So it holds the whole supply the wrong way round. At the peak that is 115 × √2 = 163 V. Its peak inverse voltage must be above that.

pages.name: How low it dips
pages.task: On 400 V the line-to-line peak is 566 V. Each top of the output runs from 30° before a peak to 30° after it. How low does the output dip?
pages.why: Each top is a slice of a cosine, from −30° to +30°. At its edges it has fallen to cos 30° = 0.866 of the peak. So the output dips only to 0.866 × 566 = 490 V.

pages.name: One diode fails
pages.task: One diode in a 230 V, 50 Hz bridge fails open. What does the load get now?
pages.answer: Half-wave: about 104 V, 50 humps a second
pages.why: The pair with the open diode can no longer carry its half. The other pair still carries its half. So the bridge works as a half-wave rectifier. The average falls to about 104 V. The humps come 50 times a second.

pages.name: Six-pulse on 440 V
pages.task: A six-pulse rectifier runs from 440 V into a resistor. What average DC does the load get?
pages.why: The average is 1.35 times the line voltage. That gives 1.35 × 440 = 594 V. The tops reach 440 × √2 = 622 V. The dips between them pull the average a little below that.
